analytical_question: How far did the Theranos proprietary multi-analyte platform, rather than the branded testing service, diffuse; what accelerated or inhibited it; and what historical timing implication followed for this organization?
general_et_finding: Theranos promoted a proprietary finger-prick multi-analyte platform, but the supplied record does not document broad verified use by independent laboratories. One FDA substantial-equivalence decision covered a specified HSV-1 IgG assay and intended use, not broad multi-analyte capability. Arizona service volume and Walgreens center counts measure access to Theranos-branded tests, not use of Edison/miniLab. The SEC alleged most patient tests used modified or standard third-party analyzers; later DOJ trial evidence describes serious analyzer failures and voided tests. Theranos was the innovating supplier and Walgreens a channel partner. A national Rogers adopter category for the proprietary platform is indeterminate from these data; calling it early majority is unsupported. In hindsight its clinical diffusion attempt failed rather than becoming a validated mainstream platform.
application_finding: Retail finger-prick multi-analyte clinical testing gained *service access*: Walgreens later closed 40 Arizona centers, and Arizona recorded about 1.5 million service tests to more than 175,000 people in 2013-2016, with about 10% voided or corrected. These counts cannot show platform penetration. Rogers factors — Relative advantage: less invasive, faster, cheaper testing was claimed, but broad accuracy and benefit were not independently established. Compatibility: clinical use required assay-specific validity, specimen integrity and CLIA-compliant laboratory processes; FDA reviewed only one specified HSV-1 assay, and its 2015 Form 483 recorded quality-system observations. Complexity: micro-volume handling, analyzer limits, quality control and third-party substitutions made the service harder than the simple marketing story. Trialability: controlled nonclinical, assay-by-assay analytical verification was possible; broad patient rollout was not a responsible trial. Observability: site and sales counts were visible while actual analyzer provenance and assay performance were opaque; later voids/corrections exposed the gap. Retail partner reach, publicity and investment accelerated attention and service access, while verification and regulatory concerns inhibited credible platform spread.

evidence.claim: FDA found substantial equivalence for Theranos HSV-1 IgG assay K143236 with specified fingerstick and venous specimen uses and Theranos system; not a general multi-assay clearance.
evidence.notes: Scope is one assay and intended use. Do not infer a broad multi-analyte platform clearance.

evidence.claim: FDA inspection recorded Nanotainer listing and complaint-handling observations.
evidence.notes: Form 483 explicitly says observations are not final agency compliance determinations.

evidence.claim: Walgreens announced termination and closure of all 40 Arizona Theranos Wellness Centers after voided results and CMS concerns.
evidence.notes: Centers delivered branded services; their count does not measure proprietary analyzer use.

evidence.claim: Arizona reported about 1.5 million Theranos tests sold to over 175,000 Arizonans in 2013-2016, with roughly 10% later voided or corrected.
evidence.evidence_type: Original state attorney-general annual report of settlement
evidence.notes: Arizona only; service transactions, not independent-lab adoption or proprietary analyzer runs.

evidence.claim: SEC alleged the proprietary analyzer handled only a small number of tests and most patient tests used modified or standard third-party analyzers.
evidence.date_or_recency: SEC litigation release March 19, 2018; checked October 24, 2026
evidence.evidence_type: Original civil enforcement release and allegations
evidence.notes: Theranos and Holmes settled without admitting or denying the allegations; label this as the SEC allegation, not a criminal conviction.

evidence.claim: DOJ reports trial evidence of analyzer failures and Theranos voiding tests run on its analyzer; it reports Balwani conviction and Holmes investor-fraud conviction.
evidence.date_or_recency: DOJ release December 2022 describing trials and prior conduct; checked October 24, 2026
evidence.evidence_type: Original federal prosecution report of trial evidence and verdicts
evidence.notes: Hindsight after the 2015 decision point. Holmes was acquitted of patient-related charges in her trial; do not collapse distinct verdicts.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: No reliable denominator or time series for external use of the proprietary Edison/miniLab multi-analyte platform is supplied; service transactions cannot establish platform adopter categories.
The FDA HSV-1 determination is narrow; it does not validate the advertised broad test menu. FDA Form 483 is an inspection observation, and SEC civil claims must be labeled allegations.
The 2017-2022 findings are retrospective evidence and should not be attributed to what a decision maker could know in 2015; contemporaneous independent assay validation is not supplied.
organization_specific_finding: Walgreens was a distribution partner, not independent proof that the Theranos analyzer worked. Its retail footprint accelerated service exposure but it lacked direct control of assay performance. Given patient and brand exposure, partner due diligence and customer transition were its immediate responsibilities; Theranos results and FDA scope remain unchanged.
confidence_and_uncertainty: High confidence that Walgreens closed all 40 Arizona centers in June 2016 and cited voids/CMS concerns; low confidence in proprietary analyzer use beneath the branded service. A hypothetical earlier suspension threshold is an inference.
value_opportunity_implication: Convenient testing could differentiate retail care if independently verified; the observed center rollout did not prove the promised diagnostic advantage.
risk_governance_implication: Require source-lab/analyzer disclosure, independent assay validity, escalation of voided results, customer transition and physician notification; partner branding cannot replace laboratory oversight.
recommendation_management_implication: For the 2015-2016 partnership review, Walgreens should have withheld further center expansion pending independent evidence and suspended affected testing as quality concerns emerged. Once voids and CMS concerns were known, terminate/transition immediately; Walgreens did announce closure of 40 Arizona centers in June 2016.
change_monitoring_triggers: Supplier delivers independently verified assay-by-assay performance and analyzer provenance.
Regulatory concerns and voided-test remediation are resolved.
Partner contract gives Walgreens audit and rapid suspension rights.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: Do not use center count as a platform adoption rate.
Do not resume patient service based only on supplier claims or one assay decision.
